nameStory: The Comb-clawed Beetle gets its name from the distinctive comb-like structure on its front legs, which looks like tiny teeth arranged in a row. These specialized 'combs' help the beetle clean its antennae and legs, much like how we might use a fine-toothed comb to groom our hair.
description: The Comb-clawed Beetle is a small, dark darkling beetle that's part of a large family known for their tough, armor-like exterior. These compact beetles typically measure about 3-5 millimeters long - roughly the size of a peppercorn. They have a distinctly oval, somewhat flattened body that's usually dark brown to blackish in color. Like all darkling beetles, they're built for durability with hard wing covers that protect their delicate flight wings underneath.

idTips.label: Comb-like front leg structures
idTips.description: Look closely at the front legs with a magnifying glass - you'll see tiny, comb-like structures that feel rigid when gently touched with a fine brush

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Small oval beetle about the size of a peppercorn, with a slightly flattened appearance that feels smooth and hard to the touch

idTips.label: Dark coloration
idTips.description: Body ranges from dark brown to sooty black, often with a subtle matte finish that doesn't reflect much light

idTips.label: Antennae structure
idTips.description: Antennae are segmented and slightly club-shaped at the tips, feeling firm when gently manipulated

idTips.label: Movement pattern
idTips.description: Moves with a characteristic slow, deliberate crawl and often plays dead when disturbed, becoming completely motionless

habitat: Comb-clawed Beetles are typically found in decaying organic matter throughout New England's forests and woodlands. Look for them under loose bark, in rotting logs, leaf litter, and compost piles where they feed on decomposing plant material. They prefer moist but well-drained areas and are often discovered when turning over fallen logs or raking through deep leaf litter in deciduous and mixed forests.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, often found under bark and in leaf litter as they emerge from winter hiding spots.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly encountered. This is the best time to spot them actively moving around decaying wood.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek winter shelter. Adults can be found preparing hibernation sites under bark and in deep leaf litter.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate in protected locations like deep under bark or buried in leaf litter, remaining dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Despite being called 'darkling' beetles, many species in this family have lost the ability to fly even though they still have wings - their wing covers have fused together, making them permanent ground-dwellers that must walk everywhere they go!
confusionNotes: Comb-clawed Beetles can be confused with other small dark beetles, but the comb-like structures on their front legs are unique - remember 'combs for cleaning' to distinguish them from similar darkling beetles that lack these specialized grooming tools.
contextualKnowledge: The family name 'Tenebrionidae' comes from the Latin word 'tenebrio' meaning 'one who loves darkness,' reflecting these beetles' preference for hiding in dark, secluded places during the day.
compareHints: [Note: Uncertain about specific comparative details for this genus] As the only Capnochroa species commonly found in New England, this beetle can be distinguished from other darkling beetles by its specialized comb-like leg structures. Most other darkling beetles in the region lack these distinctive grooming combs and tend to be either much larger or have different body proportions.
